summary: A TouchBistro blog article by Katie McCann giving restaurant owners a guide to finding and leasing a restaurant space. It covers preparing a pitch deck with financial projections, an 11-point checklist for evaluating a space (budget, location, neighborhood, size, structure, competition, accessibility, visibility, parking, safety, room to grow), and ways to search for space, including working with brokers and online listings, plus negotiation advice. The page's navigation and promotional boilerplate are excluded.
one_line: TouchBistro guide on finding and leasing restaurant real estate, covering pitch decks, an 11-point site checklist, search methods and negotiation tips.
key_facts: The article is titled 'Restaurant Real Estate: Your Guide to Finding the Right Restaurant for Lease' and is written by Katie McCann.
Los Angeles-based Restaurant Real Estate Advisors suggests a 'pitch deck' that includes at least one year of financial projections and a bio for the owner and partners if applicable.
Total occupancy cost, including rent, utilities and insurance, should not exceed 6 to 10% of gross sales, according to Restaurant Real Estate Advisors.
The article advises taking a space that costs a little less than what you think you can afford, because projections could be off and rent could rise.
Restaurant owners should visit potential sites at different times of day to analyze traffic, since a lunch crowd could become a bustling happy hour.
The max space recommended for one person is 18 square feet and the minimum is 10 square feet.
Depending on zoning, a restaurant may be required to have two to 15 parking spaces per 1,000 square feet, according to the article.
The article notes that most commercial real estate brokers work for the property owner or landlord, so their loyalty lies with the seller.
Psychology Today is cited as finding that entrepreneurs are more optimistic than non-entrepreneurs.
Nation-wide listing websites named include Loopnet.com, Bizbuysell.com and Getdigsy.com.
The article describes 'destination restaurants' as having enough appeal to draw diners from beyond their immediate community.
The article recommends hiring a professional third-party inspector to examine 'the bones' of a building, meaning its structural integrity, electrical and plumbing.
Newer building codes may require accessible entrances, exits and bathrooms, and owners should check with the local state health inspector.
The article states that a fire suppression system in the kitchen and a sprinkler system throughout the restaurant are required in many jurisdictions.
Katie McCann is a former Content Marketing Specialist at TouchBistro.
